fetched_contents.text: Parasitic Infection: Causes, Symptoms & Treatment What is a parasitic infection? Parasitic infections are any illnesses or conditions caused by parasites living and reproducing in your body. Parasites are organisms that need another living thing (a host) to get the nutrients they need to survive. Parasitic infections often cause intestinal illness, with symptoms like diarrhea and vomiting. But they can also give you itchy skin rashes or infect other parts of your body, like your brain or lungs. What are the types of parasitic infection? There are three main types of parasites that cause infections in humans: * Protozoa. * Helminths. * Ectoparasites. Protozoal infections Protozoa are single-celled parasites. They can infect your blood, intestinal tract (gut), brain, skin, eyes and other parts of your body. Helminth infections Helminth is a general term for parasitic worms. Scientists further classify them as flukes (trematodes), tapeworms (cestodes), roundworms (nematodes) and thorny-headed worms (acanthocephalans). Both adults and immature (larval) helminths can infect you. Helminths usually infect your intestinal tract, but they can also infect your skin, brain and other tissues. Ectoparasitic infections Ectoparasites are insects and arachnids (spider-like bugs) that burrow into your skin and live there. This includes ticks, mites, lice and fleas. fetched_contents.text: Diagnosis of Parasitic Diseases | Parasites * Many kinds of lab tests are available to diagnose parasitic diseases. * The kind of test(s) your health care provider will order will be based on your signs and symptoms, any other medical conditions you may have, and your travel history. * Diagnosis may be difficult, so your health care provider may order more than one kind of test. What kinds of tests are used to diagnose parasitic diseases? See below for a list of some commonly used tests your health care provider may order. A fecal (stool) exam, also called an ova and parasite test (O&P) This test is used to find parasites that cause diarrhea, loose or watery stools, cramping, flatulence (gas) and other abdominal illness. CDC recommends that three or more stool samples, collected on separate days, be examined. This test looks for ova (eggs) or the parasite. Your health care provider may instruct you to put your stool specimens into special containers with preservative fluid. Specimens not collected in a preservative fluid should be refrigerated, but not frozen, until delivered to the lab or the health care provider’s office. Your health care provider may request that the lab use special stains or that special tests be performed to look for parasites not routinely screened for. Endoscopy/Colonoscopy Endoscopy is used to find parasites that cause diarrhea, loose or watery stools, cramping, flatulence (gas) and other abdominal illness. This test is used when stool exams do not reveal the cause of your diarrhea. This test is a procedure in which a tube is inserted into the mouth (endoscopy) or rectum (colonoscopy) so that the doctor, usually a gastroenterologist, can examine the intestine. This test looks for the parasite or other abnormalities that may be causing your signs and symptoms. Blood tests Some, but not all, parasitic infections can be detected by testing your blood. Blood tests look for a specific parasite infection; there is no blood test that will look for all parasitic infections. There are two general kinds of blood tests that your doctor may order: * Serology This test is used to look for antibodies or for parasite antigens produced when the body is infected with a parasite and the immune system is trying to fight off the invader. This test is done by your health care provider taking a blood sample and sending it to a lab. * Blood smear This test is used to look for parasites that are found in the blood. By looking at a blood smear under a microscope, parasitic diseases such as filariasis, malaria, or babesiosis, can be diagnosed. This test is done by placing a drop of blood on a microscope slide. The slide is then stained and examined under a microscope. X-ray, Magnetic Resonance Imaging (MRI) scan, Computerized Axial Tomography scan (CAT) These tests are used to look for some parasitic diseases that may cause lesions in the organs. Can my lab work be sent directly to CDC? No. CDC is a reference lab for the 50 states and their individual health labs. This means that CDC cannot accept specimens unless they are sent by your state health lab. Where should lab specimens be sent for testing? Blood testing is done by a variety of labs. Your health care provider will decide where to send the blood samples to. Diagnosis of any stool parasite may be difficult; by submitting several stool specimens, your chance of being diagnosed correctly is higher than by submitting just one sample. If you receive a negative lab report, your physician may choose to send another sample to a different lab for confirmation. Is it true that labs in the United States cannot diagnose parasites? No. Labs throughout the United States are qualified to diagnose parasitic infections. Some labs have more experience than others or use various tests for the same parasite. Therefore, your health care provider may have more than one lab look at a sample if the suspicion of a parasitic infection is strong. April 9, 2024

## 1) What is the most likely cause of a chronic rash on the arm lasting weeks?

The evidence points to a common pattern: **a chronic arm rash lasting weeks is more likely to be eczema, psoriasis, or another inflammatory skin condition than a parasitic infection** [N1-R3][N4-R1][N4-R2][N4-R5]. The dermatology sources in the branch report list eczema, psoriasis, and eczema-like conditions as first-line considerations for chronic rashes, while also noting that chronic itchy rashes are often due to dermatitis or secondary to scratching [N1-R3][N4-R2]. That means eczema and psoriasis are the most likely non-parasitic explanations.

Parasitic infections are a smaller but still possible cause. The evidence says parasitic infections can cause skin rashes or itchy skin, and that some parasitic diseases can present with urticaria or allergic skin reactions [N2-R1][N2-R2]. It also notes that parasitic skin diseases can include scabies, swimmer’s itch, and other conditions [N2-R1][N2-R4][N2-R5]. So, **parasites are a plausible explanation, but not the first one**.

## 2) What parasite-related infections are associated with chronic or persistent arm rash?

The branch reports support a few specific parasitic skin conditions, but they are not exhaustive. The clearest examples in the evidence are:

- **Scabies**: caused by mites burrowing into the skin, producing an itchy, pimple-like linear rash [N2-R4].
- **Swimmer’s itch / cercarial dermatitis**: a rash caused by an allergic reaction to certain parasites found in warm bodies of water [N2-R5][N6-R4].
- **Other parasitic skin diseases**: the evidence broadly mentions parasitic infections of the skin, including creeping eruption, lice, and scabies, and notes that parasitic dermatoses can be caused by insects, worms, protozoa, or coelenterates [N2-R1][N3-R3][N6-R3].

The branch reports also note that parasitic infections can cause fever, fatigue, and intestinal symptoms, in addition to skin rash [N2-R1]. That means the rash may be part of a wider parasitic illness, not just a skin-only condition.

## 3) Which non-parasitic conditions should be considered first?

The branch reports make it clear that eczema, psoriasis, and other inflammatory dermatoses are the first considerations [N1-R3][N4-R1][N4-R2][N4-R5]. Eczema and psoriasis can look similar and are often confused by appearance alone, which is why the evidence emphasizes that a persistent rash may be more than irritation [N4-R1][N4-R2]. The general rash differential also includes bullous pemphigoid, lichen planus, and other chronic skin conditions [N1-R1]. So, the non-parasitic first-line diagnoses are broad and include:

- eczema
- psoriasis
- inflammatory dermatoses
- bullous pemphigoid
- lichen planus
- other chronic skin conditions

## 4) Can the rash pattern, location, or duration suggest a specific cause?

The evidence supports this, but with caution. For non-parasitic chronic rashes, **pattern and location help narrow the diagnosis**, but they are not enough on their own to distinguish between eczema, psoriasis, and parasitic causes [N1-R3][N4-R1]. The same sources note that chronic rashes can be hard to tell apart by appearance alone [N4-R1][N4-R2].

For parasites, the evidence is clearer for **scabies** and **swimmer’s itch**:
- Scabies typically presents with an itchy, pimple-like linear rash from mite burrowing [N2-R4].
- Swimmer’s itch is a rash caused by an allergic reaction to certain burrowing parasites [N2-R5][N6-R4].

However, the provided evidence does not give a full list of all chronic arm-specific parasitic rash patterns, so the conclusion is cautious: **pattern and location can point toward a cause, but they are not definitive without further testing** [N1-R3][N2-R4][N2-R5].

## 5) What are the signs that might point toward a parasitic infection?

The branch reports say parasitic infection is more likely if:
- the rash is persistent or recurrent
- the rash is itchy
- there is a travel history or exposure risk
- there are symptoms outside the rash, such as fever, fatigue, or digestive symptoms [N2-R1][N3-F2][N7-R1][N7-R5]

That is important because many parasitic infections are acquired through travel, contaminated food or water, or contact with animals or insects [N7-R1][N7-R5]. The evidence also emphasizes that parasitic infections can be detected by blood tests, stool tests, endoscopy, and imaging, depending on symptoms and travel/exposure history [N3-F2].

## 6) What tests can confirm or rule out parasites?

The branch reports clearly support a workup that may include:
- **blood tests**
- **stool tests / fecal exams**
- **endoscopy**
- **imaging**
- **special stains or tests** if the lab needs to look for less common parasites [N3-F2][N3-R2][N3-R4]

The evidence also says that diagnosis may be difficult and that multiple tests may be needed, especially if symptoms are not clear-cut [N3-F2]. So the main takeaway is: **do not assume a parasitic cause without testing; testing is guided by symptoms, travel history, and other conditions** [N3-F2][N3-R2][N3-R4].

## 7) What should you do next?

### When to seek urgent care versus when to wait
The branch reports say you should see a healthcare provider if:
- the rash is severe
- it won’t go away
- it keeps coming back
- it is spreading rapidly
- it is infected-looking or has pus
- it is causing severe pain, itching, or discomfort [N5-R1][N5-R2][N5-R4][N5-R5]

If the rash is **mild and persistent** but not clearly dangerous, it is still better to see a doctor soon rather than trying to treat it on your own [N1-R3][N5-R4].

### What to tell the doctor about the rash and other symptoms
You should tell the doctor:
- where the rash is
- how long it has been there
- whether it has changed in size or color
- how it feels (itchy, painful, burning)
- whether it has spread
- any other symptoms, especially fever, fatigue, or digestive symptoms
- travel history, exposure risk, and any activities that may have exposed you to parasites [N1-R3][N2-R1][N7-R5]

### Simple steps to reduce irritation or prevent spreading
The branch reports support basic skin-care steps:
- **Avoid scratching**, because it can make the rash worse and increase the risk of infection [N1-R3][N5-R4]
- **Keep the area clean and dry**
- **Avoid irritants** such as harsh soaps or lotions [N1-R3]
- **Use cool compresses or over-the-counter antihistamines only after discussing them with a doctor** [N5-R4][N5-R5]
- **Do not share towels, bedding, or clothing with others**, and clean shared items carefully [N5-R4]

## 8) Bottom line: parasite, eczema, or psoriasis?

- **Likely first explanations**: eczema, psoriasis, or other chronic inflammatory skin conditions [N1-R3][N4-R1][N4-R2][N4-R5]
- **Plausible parasitic explanations**: scabies, swimmer’s itch, and other parasitic skin diseases [N2-R1][N2-R4][N2-R5]

- **Best next step**: **see a doctor soon if the rash is severe, spreading, or not improving** [N5-R1][N5-R5]

## 9) What you should not do
Do not assume it is definitely a parasite without seeing a doctor. Do not try to treat it with strong medications or remedies on your own. Do not ignore it if it has lasted weeks. Do not ignore other symptoms such as fever or fatigue.

## 10) Final patient-friendly summary

If you have a rash on your arm that has lasted weeks and you are worried it could be a parasite, the most important message is: **seek care sooner rather than later if it is severe, spreading, or not improving, but wait for a doctor’s advice if it is mild and not obviously dangerous** [N1-R3][N5-R1][N5-R5].

- **Most likely cause**: eczema, psoriasis, or another chronic skin condition [N1-R3][N4-R1][N4-R2][N4-R5]
- **Possible parasitic causes**: scabies, swimmer’s itch, and other parasitic skin diseases [N2-R1][N2-R4][N2-R5]
- **When to see a doctor**: if the rash is severe, spreading, infected, or not improving [N5-R1][N5-R5]
